draft.title: The classical scientific approach
card: The classical scientific approach was developed by Frederick Taylor. He studied work closely to find the most efficient way to do each job.
Work is broken into simple tasks, and each task is timed and measured. Workers are trained to do the task the one best way.
Workers are paid for output, such as a rate for each item made. Taylor expected this to give them a reason to work faster.
The approach raised productivity, which is the amount produced for the effort and resources used. But it treated workers like parts of a machine, so the work could become dull and repetitive.
draft.remember: Measure and simplify the work, pay for output: more productivity, but workers are treated like machines.

a.q: Which action by a manager is the best example of the classical scientific approach?
opts: Timing each step of packing a box and setting one method
Asking staff to vote on how the team should work
Letting each worker choose their own way to pack
Holding weekly social events to lift team spirit
a.why: Timing each step and setting one best method is Taylor's approach of measuring simple tasks. Asking staff to vote or holding social events focus on people's needs, which Taylor's approach did not.
a.clue: Look for measuring tasks and one best method.

b.q: Dev runs a bakery in Bathurst. He splits loaf making into set steps, times each step, and pays staff a rate for each tray finished. Output rises, but staff say the work is dull. Which statement best explains both results?
opts: Pay drives speed, but simple tasks treat workers like machines
Pay drives speed, and simple tasks give workers more variety
Simple tasks lift morale, but pay for output slows the work
Timing gives workers more say, but pay for output bores them
b.why: Paying for each tray gives workers a reason to work faster, and timed, simple steps raise productivity. Repeating the same small task treats workers like parts of a machine, which makes the work dull. Saying the simple tasks give variety is wrong, as they do the opposite.
b.clue: Match one result to pay and the other to simple, repeated tasks.
